Oh Snap
oh SNAP
interjection (Gen X slang)
From snap, a sharp, cutting joke in the African American verbal contest variously called the dozens or snaps; to snap on someone is to roast him, and the 1994 book Snaps collected the form for a national audience. Oh, snap! — the bystander’s cry when someone lands a sharp comeback, or when something suddenly goes wrong — was common in hip-hop and urban youth speech by the early-to-mid 1990s and was revived by Millennials in the 2000s. The older English snap means a quick bite or a sudden crack.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Oh, snap! is the crowd’s cry when a comeback lands: one boy roasts another, the cut is sharp, and everyone in earshot shouts it. It can also mean simple surprise — "Oh snap, I forgot my homework" — but its home is the verbal contest, where the quickest tongue wins. The wit of the dozens is real, and the culture that sharpened it deserves credit for its speed and invention. The Christian observation is that Scripture knows exactly how sharp a tongue can be and tells us what to do with the edge. "There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health" (Pro 12:18). "Death and life are in the power of the tongue" (Pro 18:21). The apostle forbids "corrupt communication" and commands speech "good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers" (Eph 4:29). Proverbs speaks to the bystander, too: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth" (Pro 24:17). The oh snap crowd rejoices in exactly that stumble. Paul warns where the game ends: "if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another" (Gal 5:15). A father need not take the fun out of quick wit; he should aim it. Teach your son to be quick to build up, quicker to stand beside the boy being roasted, and slow to cheer when someone falls.

Webster 1828 Definition

1990s hip-hop and urban exclamation (from snap, a cutting joke in the dozens) cheering a sharp comeback or a sudden surprise; Scripture: Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth (Pro 24:17).

expand to see more

OH SNAP, interj. (Gen X slang, early-to-mid 1990s, United States) An exclamation at a sharp insult or comeback; also at any sudden surprise or mishap. "He said your jump shot looks like a sneeze? Oh, snap!"

From snap, n., a cutting joke in the verbal contest called the dozens or snaps; to snap on someone is to roast him.

Millennial revival in the 2000s; softened to a mild "oops" in everyday use.

Webster 1828: SNAP, v.t. 1. To break at once; to break short; as substances that are brittle. Breaks the doors open, snaps the locks. 2. To strike with a sharp sound. 3. To bite or seize suddenly with the teeth. 4. To break upon suddenly with sharp angry words. …

Decode for parents: when your child shouts it, someone else has usually just been cut — ask who, and whether he is all right.

Key Scripture

Pro 12:18 — "There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health."

Pro 18:21 — "Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof."

Eph 4:29 — "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers."

Pro 24:17 — "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth:"

Gal 5:15 — "But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another."

Modern Corruption

Oh snap is applause for a wound; Scripture prizes the tongue that heals and forbids gladness when another stumbles.

expand to see more

Applause for the cut. The bystander who shouts oh snap has not said anything cruel himself, but he has paid the cruelty its wages. Roasting games survive because the crowd rewards them, and the boy on the receiving end learns to laugh along while he bleeds. Solomon names the pleasure for what it is: gladness at another’s stumble (Pro 24:17). The tongue that speaks like the piercings of a sword (Pro 12:18) rarely works alone; it works for an audience.

Sharpness redeemed. Quick wit is a gift; the problem is the target. The same quickness that lands a roast can land a word "good to the use of edifying" (Eph 4:29), a defense of the weaker boy, or a ready answer to a scoffer. Paul’s warning to the Galatians is the honest end of the roasting game: those who bite and devour one another are consumed (Gal 5:15). Christ makes a man sharp for the sake of others.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Middle Dutch / Low German snappen (to bite quickly) → snap as a cutting joke in the dozens → 1990s hip-hop oh snap! → Millennial revival; Scripture: the tongue of the wise is health (Pro 12:18).

expand to see more

Middle Dutch / Low German snappen — to bite at, to seize quickly

English snap — a quick bite; a sharp crack; a curt retort

African American verbal contest: the dozens / snaps; the 1994 book Snaps

Early-to-mid 1990s hip-hop and urban speech: oh snap!; 2000s Millennial revival

Biblical tongue: piercings of a sword vs. health (Pro 12:18); bite and devour (Gal 5:15)

Usage

""He said your mixtape sounds like a dial-up modem." "Oh, snap!""

"Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth (Pro 24:17)."

"Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Pro 18:21) — even the bystander’s."
